POV review: Brizel Maadanim
desc:
📍 Location: נהרדעא 18א, בית שמש
📞 050-417-4495

Found a cholent spot hiding in a random alley — and ended up eating it off a stranger's car.

The yapchik was very oily — closer to a dip, with a fruity note I still can't explain. The Yerushalmi cholent had a crazy amount of meat for such a small bowl, but it was way too soupy, and there was a spice in there that tasted like Doritos. Perfect for a 2am cholent fix — just not a Shabbos-level bowl.

🔥 Final Rating: 7.3

title: Cholent and Chill 🍲 - S4 Ep 4: HaShteitele
desc:
📍 Location: HaRebbe MiZvehil St., corner of Baba Sali, Beitar Illit
🏷️ Hechsher: Badatz Eida Chareidis

A fully automated cholent shop — eight screens, order whatever you want, and two ladies running the whole place.

The mayo herring is a perfect kiddush herring, with a nice pepper and cilantro punch. The cholent is thick, with all the kishke and a perfect beans-to-barley ratio — it just needed a drop of salt.

If you're in Beitar, it's worth the stop.

🔥 Final Rating: 8.3

title: Cholent and Chill 🍲 - S3 Ep 11: Leil Shishi BaMoshav
desc:
📍 Location: שניר 48, נחלים

Hidden in the backyard of a school — and somehow, this is where one of the best cholents in the Merkaz lives.

The yahtzik is all asado, fully pulled, caramelized onions doing the heavy lifting — no filler, no shortcuts. Chopped liver with onion jam and cherry tomatoes — rich, high-profile. Then the cholent: barley-heavy, homemade kishka, beef fat rendered in. Perfect consistency, still lava-hot. Less than an hour from Yerushalayim. Come hungry.

🔥 Final Rating: 9.0

⚠️ This meal was complimentary, but my thoughts are my own.

title: Cholent and Chill 🍲 - S3 Ep 10: Habis Hamushlam
desc:
📍 Location: מצפה איילון, נוף איילו
🔖 Hechsher: תעודת הכשר מהדרין

The locals didn’t want me finding this one. Best view of any cholent spot I’ve been to—and somehow that’s not even the best part.

Challe schnitzel was next level—the sauce + the right challe makes all the difference. Brisket sandwich was packed with flavor, possibly smoked, and seriously good.

The cholent: barley-heavy, chunky, with a big piece of kishka, potatoes, and meat. Slightly sweet and a drop low on salt, but the consistency is perfect and the flavor is unreal—classic kiddush-style nostalgia.

Honestly, one of the best cholents I’ve had. But the real reason to come? The insane, peaceful view overlooking נוף איילון.

🔥 Final Rating: 8.4

⚠ This meal was complimentary, but my thoughts are my own.

title: Five cholent spots you should check out for your next Leil Shishi 🍲
desc:
People always ask me: “What’s the best cholent place?”
So here are five spots that are definitely worth trying.

📍 Shimale
Address: Devorah Haneviah 16, Beit Shemesh

A small spot tucked away with one of my favorite yapcheks and a great bowl of cholent.

📍 Cholent Under The Bridge
Address: Lekhi 2, Bnei Brak

Exactly what the name says. A cholent shop literally under the bridge, known for great cholent and excellent chopped liver.

📍 Bubas and Beer Shilat
Address: HaHermon 40, Shilat Industrial Area

Great atmosphere and fantastic cholent. The lamb cholent is a must.

📍 Cholent Guy
Address: Paran 15, Ramat Eshkol, Jerusalem

Started serving from a tent on Paran and now runs a shop. Known for great poppers and a barley-heavy cholent.

📍 Cholent and Mood
Address: Jaffa St 217, Jerusalem

One of my personal favorites since starting this channel. A big Leil Shishi menu and consistently great cholent.

desc:
Location📍: Hashked 69, Beit Meir
Rating🏅: 9.1

Hidden in the heart of one of Israel's most beautiful moshavim, Chontys is not your average Leil Shishi spot. We're talking barley-only cholent — no beans in sight — loaded with meat that tastes like lamb, a fat piece of kishke right in the middle, and flavors that have somehow gotten even better since our last visit.
Oh, and the schnitzel? Crunchiest I've had in a long time.
If you're tired of the noise and chaos of the city and just want phenomenal food in a calm, beautiful setting — this is your place.

title: Cholent And Chill - S3 Ep 7 Amargenstein Shabbos
desc:
📍Ha-Rav Neufeld St 4, Bnei Brak

We visit our friend Chef Meir’s apartment for a Morganstein Shabbos dinner where we taste and review his incredible homemade dishes. We start with crispy Israeli schnitzel with lemon and salt, move on to a regular kugel with an impressive dark crust that rivals overnight kugel, and dive into a thick, authentic Benei Brak cholent loaded with potatoes, beans, barley, and meat. The highlight is the tender unt rib (delmonico steak) that looks like classic kibbe cholent on the outside but tastes like a fancy restaurant dish on the inside—earning a solid 9 out of 10 rating.

title: Cholent and Chill 🍲 - S3 Ep. 7: Cholent Dvir
desc:
📍 Location: Gesher HaHayim 6, Jerusalem
🔖 Hechsher: R Yackov Cohen

If you’re looking for a hidden gem for your Thursday night outing, this is it. Tucked away in a warehouse in a random part of Jerusalem you probably didn’t even know existed, the atmosphere here is insane — every type of Jew, young and old, all coming together for one thing: cholent.

We went with their bundle feast — jachnun, kubbe, and of course the main event: the cholent.

The kubbe (with a slight Yemenite twist) was a surprising addition, but let’s be honest — we’re here for the behemoth barley-loaded cholent. Each serving comes with about half a kilo of incredibly soft, melt-in-your-mouth meat. No knife needed. The barley-heavy base is exactly what I love — rich, hearty, perfectly cooked beans, tender potatoes, solid kishka, and deep flavorful seasoning with hints of paprika and more.

Dip it in challah and you’re living right.

🔥 Final Rating: 8.8/10

Cholent and Chill 🍲 - S3 Ep 2: The CarliBar
desc:
📍 Location: Yafo 161, Jerusalem

Stumbled onto TheCarlibarr by total accident and discovered they’re serving up some serious cholent, schnitzels, and poppers.
The poppers hit different - crispy, buffalo sauce, that kick at the end that keeps you coming back. Schnitzels are perfectly crispy outside, juicy inside, with this sesame flavor that just works.
But let’s talk about what we’re really here for: the cholent. Classic homemade style, loaded with meat, that perfect kishke on top, potatoes cooked down just right. Giving it a solid 8.6/10.
Pro tip: Don’t just order one thing. Mix the schnitzels with the cholent, get that full experience, combine all those flavors. If you know, you know 😏
Worth the trip for your Thursday night cholent fix.

title: Cholent and Chill 🍲 – S3 Ep 3: Kepshuto
desc:
📍 Location: 37 S Clifton Ave, Lakewood, NJ 08701, United States

I’ve heard a lot of good things about this place, but I had to see for myself if it lives up to the hype. We’re at Kepshuto in Lakewood on a freezing Thursday night — 24°F — so you already know a hot cholent is the move.

Right away, I’m getting strong onion notes. There’s a great balance of beans and barley, and it’s a proper mush — my favorite kind of cholent. It leans sweet, with just a hint of spice. The beans are very soft, the meat is tender, and everything comes together really well.

It feels like an Israeli-style cholent with a very American twist (probably because… Lakewood). Sweet, slightly spicy, rich, and comforting. There’s even a caramelized sweetness going on. Honestly, it might be one of the best cholents I’ve had.

Served in a Styrofoam cup — first time for everything — and it’s American-sized. I really enjoyed this bowl. Could use just a bit more salt, but overall, very impressive.

Menu & Pricing:
• Medium Cholent – $7.99

title: If Thursday Night Cholent is your vibe, follow for more.
desc:
The History of Thursday Night Cholent

Cholent, a traditional Jewish stew, is a dish steeped in history, culture, and culinary innovation. Its origins trace back to the early days of Jewish communities in Eastern Europe, where it became a staple for its practicality and nourishing qualities. However, the concept of a Thursday night cholent is a more modern adaptation of this age-old tradition.

Origins of Cholent:

Cholent's history begins with Jewish dietary laws, specifically the prohibition against cooking on the Sabbath. Observant Jews needed a way to prepare a meal that would remain hot from Friday evening until the Sabbath meal on Saturday afternoon. The solution was cholent—a slow-cooked stew that could be prepared before the Sabbath and kept warm through the use of a slow cooker or covered pot.

The traditional recipe varies by region and community, but it typically includes beans, meat, potatoes, and spices. The dish reflects the availability of ingredients and the tastes of various Jewish communities. In Eastern Europe, cholent is known as "chulent" or "tshulent," while in Sephardic communities, it's called "hameen."

The Emergence of Thursday Night Cholent:

The specific tradition of Thursday Night Cholent is a more contemporary phenomenon. It reflects a blend of historical practice and modern social trends. In many Jewish communities, Thursday night has become an informal occasion for gatherings, social events, and community dinners. This night provides an opportunity to celebrate the end of the workweek and begin the Shabbat celebrations early.

Thursday Night Cholent has gained popularity as a way to bring people together for a casual meal that honors traditional cuisine while adding a modern twist. The concept embraces the idea of sharing a communal, comforting dish in a relaxed setting. It also allows for experimentation with different ingredients and flavors, reflecting the diverse culinary creativity of today’s cooks.

Cultural Significance:

Thursday Night Cholent serves as a bridge between tradition and contemporary life. It respects the roots of the cholent tradition while adapting to modern lifestyles and preferences. For many, it’s not just about the food but also about fostering community and celebrating Jewish heritage in a way that fits into today's busy schedules.

In essence, Thursday Night Cholent is a modern celebration of a timeless tradition—a way to enjoy the rich, slow-cooked flavors of cholent while making room for new social customs and gatherings.
